title: Christmas 1886
hookLine: a sentence you were never meant to hear; Thérèse overhears her tired father, and chooses not to cry
tomorrow: why would a teenager pray for a murderer she never met?

lines: A SENTENCE NOT MEANT FOR YOU.
cards: Some sentences you were never meant to hear: someone you love, tired, saying something about you in the voice people use when they think you're out of the room. Thérèse heard one. It's after Midnight Mass.

At home, her shoes wait by the fireplace, filled with little presents, the custom for the youngest. On the stairs she hears her tired father say, more or less: well, luckily this is the last year of this.
Her sister Céline sees the tears coming.

teach.b: First, the old pattern. Since her mother's death, Thérèse writes, she'd been oversensitive. She cried at small things, and then cried for having cried.
She'd tried for years to change, and couldn't. Second, the moment. On the stairs, the old Thérèse would have dissolved.

This time she held the tears back, went down, and opened her presents as joyfully as ever, as if she'd heard nothing. Her father laughed, and the night stayed happy. Third, the name she gives it: her conversion.

teach.h: IN AN INSTANT, NOT IN YEARS.
teach.b: That night, she writes, Jesus gave back the strength of soul she had lost at four and a half, and did in an instant what she hadn't managed in years.
She felt charity enter her heart: the need to forget herself to make others happy. Fourth, the nets.
She compares herself to the apostles in Luke's Gospel, who say, in the Douay-Rheims: "Master, we have laboured all the night, and have taken nothing."
Their nets stayed empty until Jesus spoke.
Hers, she says, came up full. Here's the thing to tell a friend: the turning point of a saint's life, in her own telling, is a girl deciding not to sulk over a remark about presents.

how: Catholics celebrate Christmas with Mass, some at midnight, and with family customs that differ from place to place, such as gifts left in children's shoes.

o: the night she chose not to cry, for her father
the year her family moved to a new town
her first Christmas Mass as a young nun

s: Thérèse's 'conversion' means the night she became a Catholic
she was raised Catholic. it's her name for the night her strength came back.
Thérèse overheard her father call it the last year of the Christmas shoes
he was tired, after Midnight Mass.
Thérèse says she changed that night by trying harder
she says Jesus did in an instant what she hadn't managed in years.

games.q: a friend has tried for years to stop crying at every criticism, and she's sure she's just weak. what does Thérèse's Christmas add?
o: Thérèse tried for years too; she says the strength came as a gift.
Thérèse just found more willpower, and your friend needs more too.
Thérèse shows people like that never really change, so stop trying.
games.why: Thérèse says Jesus did in an instant what she couldn't do in years. she calls it grace given, not willpower found.

practice: Name one place where sulking comes easily for you: a remark that stings, a plan that changes. Then make a one-sentence plan for next time, one thing you'll do instead, like walking into the room and asking about their day.
If you pray, you can ask for the strength Thérèse says she was given.

wordCard.voice: Christmas 1886. The night Thérèse held back her tears for her father's sake, and called it her conversion.

orig.note: New Testament Greek for love; in 1 Corinthians 13 the Douay-Rheims renders it 'charity', the word Thérèse uses here.

carryVoice: Hang onto this: strength came at christmas, in one small choice on a staircase. Sleep well.
